title_en: 1962: China on a Map in Five Colors
excerpt_en: In 1962, someone colored a map of China's relations with the world in five shades — and almost nowhere around China was white. This is that map's story, and the year that pushed China toward an independent foreign policy.
body_en:
1962 was an extraordinary year for China. That year, the Sino-Indian War broke out along the border, the Cuban Missile Crisis pushed the world to the brink of nuclear war, and relations with the Soviet Union broke down completely. It was also the year someone drew a map of China's diplomatic relations with the world — and colored the whole world in five shades.

Black, maroon, bright red, red, and white. Five colors, five attitudes. Look at the map, and there was almost no white anywhere around China.

(The header image is an AI-generated illustration recreating the look of that five-color diplomatic map — not the original 1962 map itself.)

Five Colors, One Yardstick

The map's criteria were blunt: ignore the slogans, look only at actions. Had a country fought China? Was it blockading China? And how far did the blockade go?

  • Black — direct military conflict: countries in direct military conflict with China.
  • Maroon — extremely hostile: countries imposing a full blockade on dealings with China, with military confrontation.
  • Bright red — hostile: countries imposing a large-scale blockade on dealings with China.
  • Red — hostile: countries imposing a partial blockade on dealings with China.
  • White — neutral or better: countries whose diplomatic relations with China reached a normal level or better.

With the yardstick set, the mapmaker measured the world country by country — and 1962 showed its true colors.

The Americas: Red Everywhere but Cuba

In the Americas in 1962, not a single country besides Cuba had formal diplomatic relations with China.

It was no accident. In 1954, the Organization of American States passed a resolution collectively refusing to recognize the People's Republic of China, treating communism as the core threat. By 1962, the Cuban Missile Crisis had broken out, the Americas were collectively turning against the Soviet Union, and the diplomatic blockade of China was pushed to its peak along the way.

But even in the seemingly solid Americas, there were two cracks.

Brazil pursued an independent, non-aligned foreign policy, allowing a delegation from China's trade promotion council to visit, and private trade in goods between the two countries never stopped. During the Sino-Indian conflict, Brazil did not support China — but it did not join the blockade either. It was colored red: partial blockade.

Bolivia's economy depended heavily on mineral exports, and the government did not forcibly shut down small private trade channels with China. It was colored red as well.

In other words, the red of the Americas was not a monolith. Under a U.S.-led collective blockade, two countries kept a lifeline open through private trade.

Asia: The Chessboard at China's Doorstep

Asia was where the map's colors were most complex — and it was the closest, most consequential region for China.

East Asia: Three Colors, Clearly Divided

  • Taiwan — maroon: with U.S.-supplied ships, aircraft, and weapons, it harassed the coastal areas around mainland China.
  • South Korea — maroon: under Park Chung-hee's military government, it relied on the U.S.–South Korea Mutual Defense Treaty to maintain a heavy blockade of China, with private contact completely cut off.
  • Japan — bright red: it had signed the U.S.–Japan Security Treaty and stood in the American camp, but through the 1960s it still kept private trade with China going.
  • North Korea — white: under Kim Il-sung, it leaned clearly toward China, openly supported China during the Sino-Indian conflict, and kept bilateral exchanges fully open.

Japan's box is the most interesting one: politically in the American camp, economically unwilling to cut off private trade with China. Bright red, not maroon — and that surviving private trade is the difference.

South Asia: The Only Black

In 1962, only one country in the world was colored black: India.

That year, the Sino-Indian War broke out along the border, and the two countries were in direct military conflict. Black was the heaviest color on the map — and it was given to India alone.

Beyond India, South Asia's three other neighbors took a different path. Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Nepal stayed broadly neutral and took no hostile, blockading measures against China. Bhutan, whose foreign affairs were controlled by India, imposed a partial blockade on China and was colored red.

One detail is worth noting: Pakistan was a member of both the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization (joined 1954) and the Baghdad Pact (joined 1955, later renamed the Central Treaty Organization) — two U.S.-led anti-communist military alliances, the first of which was often called "Asia's NATO" at the time — yet it supported China during the Sino-Indian conflict. Camp and stance did not line up here.

Southeast Asia: SEATO's Encirclement

Southeast Asia was colored maroon in one continuous stretch, and behind it stood one organization: the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, or SEATO.

SEATO was founded to stop the spread of communism in Southeast Asia — put more bluntly, it was an organization aimed specifically at North Vietnam and China.
  • The Philippines — maroon: a core SEATO member, it held regular U.S.–Philippine joint military exercises, allowed Taiwanese spy ships and aircraft to dock, and openly supported India during the Sino-Indian conflict.
  • Thailand — maroon: SEATO's headquarters was located there; it did not recognize the People's Republic of China, and it economically supported Taiwan's armed activities in Yunnan and backed anti-China forces.
  • South Vietnam — maroon: by the end of 1962, more than 11,300 U.S. troops were stationed there; it cooperated with the U.S. military on islands near China's Guangxi region and helped the U.S. enforce a three-way land, sea, and air blockade of China.

The three had one thing in common: U.S. military bases on their soil, and cooperation with the American blockade of China.

The rest of Southeast Asia was a mixed picture. Laos was in civil war, its three factions split: the armed forces of the coalition transitional government stayed neutral toward China, while some factions, backed by the United States, took an anti-China line. Burma and Cambodia, governed by Ne Win and Sihanouk, took an officially neutral diplomatic stance. Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak, Sabah, and Brunei were tightly constrained by a series of treaties with Britain and could not conduct diplomacy with China on their own.

The most thought-provoking case is Indonesia. Under Sukarno, Indonesia was constrained by a tangle of domestic and external factors and never drew close to China; it was colored red. That failure to draw close would echo through later history — the September 30th Movement of 1965, and the severing of China–Indonesia relations in 1967.

The Former "Big Brother": The Soviet Bloc

On the 1962 map, the Soviet Union was bright red.

That stings. Ten years earlier, the Soviet Union had been the "big brother," the object of a one-sided alliance. In six years, the relationship had turned upside down.

  • 1956: At the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, Khrushchev denounced Stalin wholesale, and the ideological split between China and the Soviet Union became public.
  • Around 1958: The Soviet Union proposed joint fleet and long-wave radio station arrangements that touched on Chinese sovereignty; China refused, and mutual trust broke down further.
  • 1962: When the Sino-Indian conflict broke out, the Soviet Union openly supported India and provided military aid; the same year, it instigated the Tacheng incident and the Yining riots in Xinjiang.

From ideological disagreement, to a contest over sovereignty, to standing on the opposite side in the Sino-Indian conflict and stirring up unrest on the frontier — the Soviet Union's bright red was added one layer at a time.

The Soviet satellites were no exception. Mongolia, a Soviet satellite, adopted an anti-China line in step with Moscow, though private exchanges between China and Mongolia survived — so it was colored red. Most other Warsaw Pact states followed the Soviet line against China; only Albania and Romania refused to obey Moscow's instructions, and Albania's position was close to China's.

Even inside the camp, it was not a monolith.

Europe and the Middle East: Light Through the Cracks

Europe and the Middle East were among the few places on the map with any white. And that white usually had nothing to do with the United States — sometimes it came from defying it.

Portugal was white. In 1961, India seized Goa by force after centuries of Portuguese rule, and Britain and the United States did nothing. Portugal was furious. When the Sino-Indian conflict broke out in 1962, Portugal openly supported China. For that same reason, Portuguese Timor stayed neutral in 1962.

France was red. Although a NATO member, France had long resented American interference. After the Algerian War ended in 1962, relations between China and France thawed. Two years later, in 1964, China and France formally established diplomatic relations — a step in France's move away from the U.S.–Soviet bipolar order.

The Middle East was churning too. North Yemen established friendly relations with China after its 1962 revolution, and bilateral exchanges flowed smoothly. Bahrain, Qatar, and the Trucial States (today's UAE) were all British protectorates, imposing a large-scale blockade on China on British orders — bright red. Oman, where the Dhofar War against British colonial rule broke out in 1962, was also bright red: China supported the anti-colonial rebels. Iran, after the Shah deposed Mossadegh's government, joined the Baghdad Pact, aligned with the United States against the Soviet Union, and took a hostile line toward China in step — but by 1971, seeking a common front against the Soviet Union, Iran's relations with China warmed rapidly.

Africa: The Silent Continent

In 1962, Africa was almost silent on this map. Most of its countries were still colonies or deeply controlled by great powers, and had not yet had a chance to express a color of their own.

But nine years later, Africa spoke. In 1971, when the People's Republic of China regained its seat at the United Nations, Africa cast the most votes against the motion — 15 in all. A silent continent is not a continent without a position.

1962 at a Glance

  • Black: India
  • Maroon: Taiwan, South Korea, the Philippines, Thailand, South Vietnam
  • Bright red: Japan, the Soviet Union, Bahrain, Qatar, the Trucial States (today's UAE), Oman
  • Red: Brazil, Bolivia, Bhutan, Mongolia, Indonesia, France
  • White: Cuba, North Korea, Portugal, North Yemen

In addition, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Nepal, Burma, and Cambodia stayed neutral and took no hostile, blockading measures against China; in Laos, the factions in the civil war were split; and Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak, Sabah, and Brunei were constrained by British treaties and could not conduct diplomacy with China on their own.

Epilogue: From "Leaning to One Side" to an Independent Foreign Policy

In 1962, China faced a blockade from both the American and Soviet blocs at once. To the east, U.S. military bases and SEATO's encirclement; to the west, a former ally that had turned its guns around. Red pressed in from every direction on the map, and white was down to a few scattered dots.

But it was also in this year that China abandoned its policy of "leaning to one side."

1962 was an extraordinary year for China. The dual blockade by the American and Soviet blocs pushed China to abandon its one-sided policy and set out on the long road to an independent foreign policy.

That five-color map did not draw an end point. It drew a starting point. From that year on, China's diplomacy would no longer lean on any camp — it would find its own way, one step at a time.
